title: Purification
hookLine: the hundred-syllable mantra of Vajrasattva, for purifying past wrongs

lines: LIKE THE MOON FREED FROM CLOUDS.
cards: "He whose evil deeds are covered by good deeds, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." That's the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation.

Tradition links the verse to Angulimala, the feared bandit you met back in year one, who met the Buddha and became a monk. The verse doesn't say the moon was never dim. It says clouds pass, and light comes back.
Tibetan practice has a whole method for those clouds, for things a person has done and can't undo. It's the second of the four foundations, and it centers on a figure in white.

teach.b: First, Vajrasattva. In the practice texts he's pictured seated above the practitioner's head, white as moonlight, holding a vajra and a bell.
His name is usually rendered something like diamond being, and Tibetan teachers present him as the purity of all the buddhas in one form. Second, the mantra.

teach.h: NECTAR POURS, THE DARK WASHES OUT.
teach.b: His long hundred-syllable mantra is recited again and again while the practitioner pictures bright nectar pouring down from him, through the crown, filling the body.
Old wrongs and harms leave as dark liquid, washed down and out. Third, the four powers.

Gampopa and other Tibetan teachers say purification rests on four supports: honest regret for what was done, reliance on refuge and on the wish to help others, the remedy itself, like the mantra, and the resolve not to do it again.
Notice what isn't on the list: punishing yourself. Regret here means seeing clearly, not sinking. Fourth, washed clean.
In versions of the practice, Vajrasattva declares at the end that the practitioner's wrongs are purified, then dissolves into light that melts into them.
Teachers explain the logic with a picture close to the Dhammapada's: the stains are like clouds, not the moon itself.

The mind underneath, they say, was never ruined. In their telling, purification doesn't erase the past. It loosens the past's grip on the present, so a person can stand in the light again and choose differently.

how: In the Tibetan foundational practices, students recite Vajrasattva's hundred-syllable mantra many times while visualizing purifying nectar, relying on the four powers of regret, reliance, remedy and resolve.

o: clearing past wrongs through regret, a remedy and resolve
punishing yourself until the guilt finally goes away
a ritual bath taken before entering a temple

p: white, above the head, vajra and bell
pours down and washes out the dark
resolve not to do it again
a bandit who became a monk

s: the four powers include punishing yourself
they're regret, reliance, the remedy and resolve. regret means seeing clearly, not sinking.
the Dhammapada compares the changed person to the moon freed from clouds
the clouds pass, and the light comes back.
purification erases the past as if it never happened
it loosens the past's grip on the present, so a person can choose differently.

games.q: you've done something you regret, and you've come to the Vajrasattva practice. you've looked at it honestly and recited the mantra. what's the last step teachers name?
o: punish yourself until it feels paid.
resolve not to do it again.
games.why: the four powers end with resolve, after regret, reliance and the remedy. self-punishment isn't one of them.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you wish you hadn't done, not the worst thing, just a real one, and look at it honestly for a moment, without arguing and without punishing.

Then picture something clear and cool pouring down over you, like water or light, and let the heaviness run out with each breath out. At the end, quietly make one small resolve about what you'd do differently.

wordCard.voice: Purification. In the Tibetan foundations, Vajrasattva's practice: honest regret, a remedy, and resolve, until the clouds pass. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit Vajrasattva: usually rendered 'diamond being', the figure of purity at the heart of this practice.

carryVoice: Your line: washed clean. Clouds pass, and the moon was never ruined. See you tomorrow.
